items.title: I can define person perception and distinguish between direct and indirect sources of information
items.what: Person perception refers to the mental processes used to understand and form impressions of others. Information can come directly from the person through observation or interaction, or indirectly through a third party such as a friend's description or an online profile.
items.why: Recognising the source of our impressions helps us assess their reliability. Indirect information is filtered through another person's interpretation and may be less accurate than direct observation.
items.example: You observe a classmate sleeping in class (direct perception). Later, a friend tells you that classmate is lazy and unmotivated (indirect perception). Your final impression is shaped by both sources, but the indirect source may be biased.

subtopic.name: Person Perception and Attributions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how we form mental impressions of other people and how we decide what caused their behaviour. It covers direct and indirect perception, first impressions, and the three-step cognitive process of attribution.
subtopic.why: Understanding how we perceive and judge others helps explain why interpersonal conflicts arise, why we sometimes misjudge people, and how our social decisions are shaped by mental shortcuts rather than objective facts.

items.title: I can explain what a first impression is and describe its influence on decision-making and interpersonal interactions
items.what: A first impression is a snap judgement formed within less than a second of meeting someone, based on easily accessible surface information such as appearance and body language. These impressions can persist and influence later behaviour toward that person.
items.why: First impressions affect who we choose to interact with, whether we offer someone a job, and how much trust we extend to a stranger. Understanding their influence helps explain why initial judgements can be unfair and hard to revise.
items.example: A job interviewer immediately forms a positive impression of a candidate who makes eye contact, sits upright, and is dressed formally. This first impression influences the interviewer's decision to shortlist the candidate before asking a single question.

subtopic.name: Person Perception and Attributions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how we form mental impressions of other people and how we decide what caused their behaviour. It covers direct and indirect perception, first impressions, and the three-step cognitive process of attribution.
subtopic.why: Understanding how we perceive and judge others helps explain why interpersonal conflicts arise, why we sometimes misjudge people, and how our social decisions are shaped by mental shortcuts rather than objective facts.

items.title: I can outline the three steps in the cognitive process of attribution
items.what: Attribution involves three ordered steps: first, observing a behaviour; second, consciously acknowledging what the behaviour was; and third, deciding on a cause for that behaviour. This process occurs constantly as we try to make sense of the actions of people around us.
items.why: Understanding the steps in attribution clarifies that the judgements we make about causes are interpretive, not factual. At step three, different people can assign very different causes to the exact same observed behaviour.
items.example: You see a student yelling in a corridor (step 1). You register that they are shouting angrily (step 2). You conclude they must be aggressive or rude by nature (step 3), even though they may have just received very bad news.

subtopic.name: Person Perception and Attributions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how we form mental impressions of other people and how we decide what caused their behaviour. It covers direct and indirect perception, first impressions, and the three-step cognitive process of attribution.
subtopic.why: Understanding how we perceive and judge others helps explain why interpersonal conflicts arise, why we sometimes misjudge people, and how our social decisions are shaped by mental shortcuts rather than objective facts.

items.title: I can distinguish between internal and external attributions and provide examples of each
items.what: Internal (personal) attributions assign the cause of behaviour to something within the individual, such as their personality, ability, or motivation. External (situational) attributions assign the cause to factors outside the individual, such as the environment, circumstances, or other people's actions.
items.why: The type of attribution made has real consequences for how we treat others and how we respond to our own failures or successes. Internal attributions can lead to blame, while external attributions can foster empathy.
items.example: A colleague arrives late to a meeting. An internal attribution: they are disorganised and don't value others' time. An external attribution: there was an unexpected road closure on their route. The same behaviour receives a fundamentally different explanation.

subtopic.name: Person Perception and Attributions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how we form mental impressions of other people and how we decide what caused their behaviour. It covers direct and indirect perception, first impressions, and the three-step cognitive process of attribution.
subtopic.why: Understanding how we perceive and judge others helps explain why interpersonal conflicts arise, why we sometimes misjudge people, and how our social decisions are shaped by mental shortcuts rather than objective facts.

items.title: I can define the fundamental attribution error and explain why it occurs
items.what: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to explain other people's behaviour using internal factors while overlooking possible external causes. It arises because when observing someone else, the person themselves is the most visually salient feature, not the situation they are in.
items.why: This error is one of the most common sources of misjudgement in social life. It can cause us to unfairly blame individuals for circumstances largely beyond their control, affecting both personal relationships and professional settings.
items.example: A shopper snaps at a cashier. An observer attributes this to the shopper being a rude and unkind person (internal), ignoring the possibility that the shopper just received devastating news about a family member (external).

subtopic.name: Person Perception and Attributions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how we form mental impressions of other people and how we decide what caused their behaviour. It covers direct and indirect perception, first impressions, and the three-step cognitive process of attribution.
subtopic.why: Understanding how we perceive and judge others helps explain why interpersonal conflicts arise, why we sometimes misjudge people, and how our social decisions are shaped by mental shortcuts rather than objective facts.

items.title: I can describe what an attributional style is and explain how it can influence future behaviour
items.what: Attributional style refers to the consistent pattern in the types of attributions a person tends to make. Someone who habitually attributes failure to stable internal factors, such as believing they are simply bad at something, may develop learned helplessness and stop trying to improve.
items.why: Research in educational psychology shows that students who attribute failure to changeable internal causes, such as insufficient effort, are more likely to improve than those who attribute it to fixed causes. Recognising one's own attributional style can be a tool for personal development.
items.example: A student who fails a chemistry test and thinks 'I am just not a science person and never will be' has a pessimistic, stable attributional style. A student who thinks 'I did not study the right sections this time' has an unstable internal attribution and is more likely to change their approach.

subtopic.name: Person Perception and Attributions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how we form mental impressions of other people and how we decide what caused their behaviour. It covers direct and indirect perception, first impressions, and the three-step cognitive process of attribution.
subtopic.why: Understanding how we perceive and judge others helps explain why interpersonal conflicts arise, why we sometimes misjudge people, and how our social decisions are shaped by mental shortcuts rather than objective facts.

items.title: I can define attitude and state the three criteria required for a belief to qualify as an established attitude
items.what: An attitude is an evaluation of something, such as a person, object, event, or idea. For a belief to qualify as an established attitude it must be: (1) an evaluation of something (placed on a positive-to-negative scale), (2) settled and stable over time, and (3) learnt through experience.
items.why: The criteria distinguish attitudes from fleeting opinions or neutral observations. This distinction matters because attitudes carry motivational weight: they guide consistent patterns of behaviour in ways that brief judgements do not.
items.example: Believing that huskies are an energetic dog breed is not an attitude because no evaluative judgement is being made. Believing huskies are the best dog breed ever is an attitude: it is a positive evaluation, it is stable, and it was likely formed through personal experience with the breed.

subtopic.name: Attitudes and Stereotypes
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what attitudes are, the three criteria for an established attitude, and the tri-component (A-B-C) model that maps the affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions of any attitude. It also addresses stereotypes as the cognitive component of attitudes toward social groups.
subtopic.why: Attitudes shape nearly every social decision we make, from what we eat to who we befriend to how we vote. Understanding their structure and how they can be inconsistent helps explain both individual behaviour and broader social patterns.

items.title: I can identify and describe each component of the tri-component model of attitudes
items.what: The tri-component (A-B-C) model proposes that attitudes have three interconnected components. The affective component is our emotional or intuitive feeling toward something. The behavioural component is the observable action that reflects the attitude. The cognitive component comprises our thoughts and beliefs about something.
items.why: The model provides a structured way to analyse any attitude in full. It also helps explain why attitudes can be expressed inconsistently, since not all three components need to align in practice.
items.example: Regarding factory farming: affective — feeling disgusted by the conditions animals are kept in; cognitive — believing that factory farming causes unnecessary suffering; behavioural — choosing not to buy products from companies known to use factory farming.

subtopic.name: Attitudes and Stereotypes
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what attitudes are, the three criteria for an established attitude, and the tri-component (A-B-C) model that maps the affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions of any attitude. It also addresses stereotypes as the cognitive component of attitudes toward social groups.
subtopic.why: Attitudes shape nearly every social decision we make, from what we eat to who we befriend to how we vote. Understanding their structure and how they can be inconsistent helps explain both individual behaviour and broader social patterns.

items.title: I can give examples of affective, behavioural, and cognitive statements about the same attitude
items.what: The affective component is expressed through feeling language (e.g. 'I feel'), the cognitive component through belief language (e.g. 'I think/believe'), and the behavioural component through action (e.g. observable conduct). All three can refer to the same attitude object but describe it from a different angle.
items.why: Being able to identify which component a statement reflects is a core exam skill and helps clarify the often-blurry boundary between emotion and rational thought in our social judgements.
items.example: About wearing school uniforms — affective: 'I feel annoyed when I have to wear a uniform.' Cognitive: 'I believe uniforms suppress individual expression.' Behavioural: rolling up the sleeves of the uniform to slightly personalise it.

subtopic.name: Attitudes and Stereotypes
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what attitudes are, the three criteria for an established attitude, and the tri-component (A-B-C) model that maps the affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions of any attitude. It also addresses stereotypes as the cognitive component of attitudes toward social groups.
subtopic.why: Attitudes shape nearly every social decision we make, from what we eat to who we befriend to how we vote. Understanding their structure and how they can be inconsistent helps explain both individual behaviour and broader social patterns.

items.title: I can outline a key limitation of the tri-component model and explain it using an example
items.what: A significant limitation of the tri-component model is that the behavioural component may not reflect the affective and cognitive components. Many psychologists argue that an attitude can exist with only the affective and cognitive components present, because behaviour is not always able to express the underlying attitude.
items.why: This limitation is directly relevant to cognitive dissonance. It shows that attitudes do not mechanically produce matching behaviour, and that understanding a person's feelings and thoughts is not sufficient to predict what they will do.
items.example: A person genuinely believes (cognitive) and feels (affective) that a child at a family gathering is irritating and rude. However, they smile warmly and play along (behaviour) out of respect for the child's parents. The behaviour is entirely inconsistent with the other two components.

subtopic.name: Attitudes and Stereotypes
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what attitudes are, the three criteria for an established attitude, and the tri-component (A-B-C) model that maps the affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions of any attitude. It also addresses stereotypes as the cognitive component of attitudes toward social groups.

items.title: I can define a stereotype and explain its relationship to the cognitive component of attitudes
items.what: A stereotype is a widely held, oversimplified generalisation about all members of a group. Because stereotypes are beliefs about a category of people, they function as the cognitive component of our attitudes toward that group.
items.why: Stereotypes form the cognitive foundation that can later generate emotional prejudice (affective) and discriminatory behaviour (behavioural). Recognising that stereotypes are beliefs, not facts, is the starting point for understanding and reducing prejudice.
items.example: The stereotype that scientists are introverted men who wear glasses and work only in labs may cause a person to dismiss a female field ecologist as not being a 'real' scientist, despite her qualifications and published research.

subtopic.name: Attitudes and Stereotypes
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers what attitudes are, the three criteria for an established attitude, and the tri-component (A-B-C) model that maps the affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions of any attitude. It also addresses stereotypes as the cognitive component of attitudes toward social groups.
subtopic.why: Attitudes shape nearly every social decision we make, from what we eat to who we befriend to how we vote. Understanding their structure and how they can be inconsistent helps explain both individual behaviour and broader social patterns.

items.title: I can explain how stereotypes influence decision-making and interpersonal interactions
items.what: Stereotypes influence which goals we set for ourselves, who we choose to interact with, and how we behave toward others. They cause us to focus on features of individuals that match the group stereotype and overlook features that contradict it.
items.why: Stereotypes create a feedback loop: they shape interactions in ways that can appear to confirm the original stereotype, making them resistant to change even in the face of contradictory evidence.
items.example: A student who believes that 'people like me don't do well in maths' (a stereotype about their demographic group) may avoid selecting advanced mathematics subjects, limiting their career options before any actual academic evidence exists.

It also addresses stereotypes as the cognitive component of attitudes toward social groups.
subtopic.why: Attitudes shape nearly every social decision we make, from what we eat to who we befriend to how we vote. Understanding their structure and how they can be inconsistent helps explain both individual behaviour and broader social patterns.

items.title: I can define cognitive dissonance and identify the conditions under which it occurs
items.what: Cognitive dissonance is the psychological tension experienced when our thoughts, feelings, and/or behaviours do not align with one another. It is most likely to occur when a person was aware of the potential consequences of their behaviour before acting and cannot adequately justify why they acted that way.
items.why: Not every inconsistency produces cognitive dissonance. Understanding the conditions under which it occurs prevents overapplication of the concept and helps identify genuinely dissonance-producing situations in exam scenarios.
items.example: A student who values academic success (thought) stays up watching television until 2 a.m. the night before an exam (behaviour). Because they knew the consequences and had no justification, they feel uncomfortable and unsettled. A student who stayed up late because of a family emergency would be less likely to feel dissonance, since the behaviour was justifiable.

subtopic.name: Cognitive Dissonance and Cognitive Biases
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the psychological discomfort that arises when our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are inconsistent, and the unconscious mental strategies we use to reduce that discomfort. Five specific cognitive biases are covered: confirmation bias, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias, false-consensus bias, and the halo effect.
subtopic.why: Cognitive dissonance and the biases used to reduce it operate largely below conscious awareness, yet they influence major life decisions, shape self-image, and affect how fairly we treat others. Understanding them is a prerequisite for more honest self-reflection.

items.title: I can explain the two primary ways cognitive dissonance can be reduced
items.what: Cognitive dissonance is most directly reduced by either changing the behaviour to align with the thought, or changing the thought to align with the behaviour. Both strategies restore internal consistency and eliminate the feeling of tension.
items.why: Knowing these two direct reduction strategies sets the foundation for understanding cognitive biases, which serve as a third, more indirect pathway that allows people to avoid resolving the underlying inconsistency at all.
items.example: A person believes that regular exercise is essential for health (thought) but has not exercised in three months (behaviour). They can reduce dissonance by starting an exercise routine (change behaviour) or by revising their belief to 'exercise is helpful but not strictly necessary for everyone' (change thought).

subtopic.name: Cognitive Dissonance and Cognitive Biases
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the psychological discomfort that arises when our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are inconsistent, and the unconscious mental strategies we use to reduce that discomfort. Five specific cognitive biases are covered: confirmation bias, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias, false-consensus bias, and the halo effect.
subtopic.why: Cognitive dissonance and the biases used to reduce it operate largely below conscious awareness, yet they influence major life decisions, shape self-image, and affect how fairly we treat others. Understanding them is a prerequisite for more honest self-reflection.

items.title: I can define cognitive biases and explain their role in reducing cognitive dissonance
items.what: Cognitive biases are unconscious, systematic tendencies to interpret information in ways that are neither rational nor based on objective reality. They function as a third pathway for reducing cognitive dissonance by distorting how information is processed so that the inconsistency feels less severe.
items.why: Because cognitive biases operate unconsciously, people typically do not recognise when they are using them. This makes them particularly influential and difficult to correct without deliberate effort.
items.example: A person who smokes but knows smoking is harmful does not quit (the inconsistency remains) but instead gravitates toward news stories that question anti-smoking research. The bias lets them maintain the inconsistency while feeling less tension about it.

Five specific cognitive biases are covered: confirmation bias, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias, false-consensus bias, and the halo effect.

items.title: I can define confirmation bias and apply it to a scenario
items.what: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek out, notice, and accept information that supports existing beliefs or behaviours, while ignoring or discounting information that contradicts them.
items.why: Confirmation bias is one of the most extensively documented biases in psychology and has implications beyond individual wellbeing, influencing political polarisation, medical self-diagnosis, and corporate decision-making.
items.example: A person believes that a particular diet is uniquely effective for weight loss. When they read a scientific review concluding the diet has no special benefit over other calorie-controlled approaches, they dismiss it as biased. When they find a single blog post praising the diet, they share it widely.

subtopic.name: Cognitive Dissonance and Cognitive Biases
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the psychological discomfort that arises when our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are inconsistent, and the unconscious mental strategies we use to reduce that discomfort. Five specific cognitive biases are covered: confirmation bias, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias, false-consensus bias, and the halo effect.
subtopic.why: Cognitive dissonance and the biases used to reduce it operate largely below conscious awareness, yet they influence major life decisions, shape self-image, and affect how fairly we treat others. Understanding them is a prerequisite for more honest self-reflection.

items.title: I can define actor-observer bias and distinguish it from the fundamental attribution error
items.what: Actor-observer bias is the tendency to attribute one's own actions to external, situational factors while attributing other people's actions to internal, dispositional factors. It differs from the fundamental attribution error in that the fundamental attribution error applies only to judgements about others, whereas actor-observer bias captures the asymmetry between self-attribution and other-attribution.
items.why: This bias helps explain why interpersonal conflicts often feel irresolvable: each party believes their own behaviour was forced by circumstances while the other person's was freely chosen and revealing of their character.
items.example: In a heated argument, Person A thinks: 'I only raised my voice because they kept interrupting me (external). They raised their voice because they are aggressive and lack self-control (internal).' Person B thinks the same thing in reverse.

subtopic.name: Cognitive Dissonance and Cognitive Biases
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the psychological discomfort that arises when our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are inconsistent, and the unconscious mental strategies we use to reduce that discomfort. Five specific cognitive biases are covered: confirmation bias, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias, false-consensus bias, and the halo effect.
subtopic.why: Cognitive dissonance and the biases used to reduce it operate largely below conscious awareness, yet they influence major life decisions, shape self-image, and affect how fairly we treat others. Understanding them is a prerequisite for more honest self-reflection.

items.title: I can define self-serving bias and explain how it reduces cognitive dissonance
items.what: Self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute successes to internal factors such as talent and effort, while attributing failures to external factors such as bad luck or unfair conditions. This protects self-esteem and reduces the dissonance that would arise from acknowledging personal responsibility for poor outcomes.
items.why: While self-serving bias can protect psychological wellbeing in the short term, it prevents accurate self-assessment and learning from failure. In professional contexts it can erode trust and impede team functioning.
items.example: A sales representative who closes a major deal attributes it to their persuasive skill and hard work. When they lose a client, they attribute it to the client's unrealistic expectations and the state of the market, not to any weakness in their own performance.

Five specific cognitive biases are covered: confirmation bias, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias, false-consensus bias, and the halo effect.
subtopic.why: Cognitive dissonance and the biases used to reduce it operate largely below conscious awareness, yet they influence major life decisions, shape self-image, and affect how fairly we treat others. Understanding them is a prerequisite for more honest self-reflection.

items.title: I can define false-consensus bias and provide a relevant example
items.what: False-consensus bias is the tendency to overestimate the extent to which other people share our own beliefs, attitudes, and behaviours. By assuming that our views are typical or widely held, we make our own position feel more valid and reduce the dissonance that might arise from holding a minority view.
items.why: False-consensus bias can reinforce political and social echo chambers. Believing that most people agree with you reduces the motivation to seek out diverse perspectives or question the accuracy of your own views.
items.example: A person who is strongly opposed to a local development project assumes that the majority of their community shares this view. When the proposal passes a community vote with 65% support, they are genuinely surprised and struggle to accept the result.

Five specific cognitive biases are covered: confirmation bias, actor-observer bias, self-serving bias, false-consensus bias, and the halo effect.
subtopic.why: Cognitive dissonance and the biases used to reduce it operate largely below conscious awareness, yet they influence major life decisions, shape self-image, and affect how fairly we treat others. Understanding them is a prerequisite for more honest self-reflection.

items.title: I can define the halo effect and explain how it is used to avoid cognitive dissonance
items.what: The halo effect is the tendency for a positive (or negative) impression formed about one quality of a person to influence overall beliefs about their other qualities. By extending a favourable first impression across all attributes, the person avoids the dissonance that would arise from holding contradictory beliefs about someone they like.
items.why: The halo effect has well-documented impacts in employment (attractive candidates rated as more competent), education (teachers rating well-behaved students as more academically able), and the justice system (physically appealing defendants receiving lighter sentences in some studies).
items.example: A new manager is extremely well-organised and punctual. A team member who notices this assumes the manager must also be a skilled communicator, a fair decision-maker, and a good mentor, before observing any evidence of these qualities.

items.title: I can define heuristics and explain how they differ from algorithms
items.what: Heuristics are information-processing strategies or mental shortcuts that allow individuals to form judgements, make decisions, and solve problems quickly and efficiently. Unlike algorithms, which are systematic step-by-step procedures that always yield a correct answer, heuristics are fast and intuitive but prone to error.
items.why: The contrast with algorithms clarifies both the value and the cost of heuristics. Speed comes at the price of accuracy. Knowing this helps us understand when to slow down and apply more deliberate analysis instead of relying on intuition.
items.example: Finding orange juice in a supermarket using an algorithm means checking every single shelf systematically until it is found. Using a heuristic means heading directly to the juice aisle based on past experience. The heuristic is faster but fails if the juice has been moved to a refrigerated section.

subtopic.name: Heuristics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers heuristics as mental shortcuts used to make quick judgements, decisions, and solve problems. Four specific heuristics are examined in detail: the anchoring heuristic, the availability heuristic, the representative heuristic, and the affect heuristic.
subtopic.why: Heuristics underlie a vast range of everyday decisions, from choosing what to eat to how we assess risk. Understanding their positive and negative influences reveals why human decision-making is simultaneously efficient and prone to systematic error.

items.title: I can identify both positive and negative influences of heuristics on decision-making and problem-solving
items.what: Positive influences of heuristics include saving time, often producing accurate outcomes, and protecting individuals from danger through fast adaptive responses. Negative influences include being prone to error, producing biased judgements, and contributing to the base-rate fallacy, where vivid personal experiences override statistical evidence.
items.why: Neither universally praising nor dismissing heuristics reflects the evidence. A balanced understanding is necessary for evaluating specific situations and for exam questions that ask for both sides of heuristic influence.
items.example: Positive: a doctor rapidly rules out rare tropical diseases in a patient who has never left Australia, focusing on more likely diagnoses and saving time. Negative: after a highly publicised shark attack, beachgoers overestimate shark risk, ignoring statistics showing car accidents are many times more likely to cause death.

subtopic.name: Heuristics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers heuristics as mental shortcuts used to make quick judgements, decisions, and solve problems. Four specific heuristics are examined in detail: the anchoring heuristic, the availability heuristic, the representative heuristic, and the affect heuristic.

items.title: I can define the anchoring heuristic and explain its influence on decision-making
items.what: The anchoring heuristic involves forming judgements based on the first piece of information received, which acts as a mental anchor. Subsequent judgements adjust away from the anchor insufficiently, so the initial value exerts a disproportionate influence on the final decision.
items.why: Anchoring is systematically exploited in pricing, salary negotiation, and legal sentencing. Recognising it as a heuristic rather than a rational process allows individuals to correct for it by deliberately generating their own reference points before receiving external ones.
items.example: A hiring manager is told a candidate's previous salary was $120,000. Even after hearing that market rates for the role are $85,000–$95,000, the manager anchors to $120,000 and offers $105,000, higher than the objective evidence would support.

subtopic.name: Heuristics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers heuristics as mental shortcuts used to make quick judgements, decisions, and solve problems. Four specific heuristics are examined in detail: the anchoring heuristic, the availability heuristic, the representative heuristic, and the affect heuristic.
subtopic.why: Heuristics underlie a vast range of everyday decisions, from choosing what to eat to how we assess risk. Understanding their positive and negative influences reveals why human decision-making is simultaneously efficient and prone to systematic error.

items.title: I can define the availability heuristic and explain the base-rate fallacy as it applies to this heuristic
items.what: The availability heuristic involves making judgements or decisions based on how easily relevant information comes to mind. The base-rate fallacy occurs within this heuristic when vivid, easily recalled examples (often from personal experience or media) override statistical base rates, leading to inaccurate assessments of probability.
items.why: Media coverage is inherently selective and dramatic, meaning the events that are most easily recalled are often the least statistically representative. Understanding availability bias helps explain widespread irrational fears, such as greater fear of flying than driving despite driving being statistically more dangerous.
items.example: After seeing repeated news coverage of a rare but dramatic bridge collapse, a person decides to avoid bridges entirely and takes a route that is 40 minutes longer, even though the statistical probability of a bridge collapse on their commute is negligibly small compared to other travel risks.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers heuristics as mental shortcuts used to make quick judgements, decisions, and solve problems. Four specific heuristics are examined in detail: the anchoring heuristic, the availability heuristic, the representative heuristic, and the affect heuristic.
subtopic.why: Heuristics underlie a vast range of everyday decisions, from choosing what to eat to how we assess risk. Understanding their positive and negative influences reveals why human decision-making is simultaneously efficient and prone to systematic error.

items.title: I can define the representative heuristic and explain its relationship to stereotypes
items.what: The representative heuristic involves judging something by how closely it resembles a typical member of a category, rather than considering actual probability or base rates. In social contexts, this heuristic relies heavily on stereotypes as the template against which individuals are compared.
items.why: The representative heuristic is a core mechanism through which stereotypes translate into real-world misjudgements and discriminatory decisions. It explains why highly qualified individuals can be overlooked for roles when their appearance does not match the stereotypical image of the role.
items.example: An interviewer for a software engineering position meets a candidate who is quietly spoken, wears casual clothes, and carries a tote bag with a video game logo. The interviewer rates the candidate as highly competent before reviewing qualifications, because the candidate matches the mental template of a software engineer.

items.title: I can define the affect heuristic and describe its influence on risk assessment and decision-making
items.what: The affect heuristic involves using current emotional state to guide judgements and decisions. A strong emotional response, such as fear, disgust, or excitement, shapes assessments of risk, value, and appropriateness, often independently of rational analysis.
items.why: The affect heuristic can be adaptive: fear of genuinely dangerous situations may protect survival. However, it can also lead to decisions that are driven by irrelevant emotional states, such as making a financial decision while elated or avoiding a beneficial opportunity due to anxiety.
items.example: A student receives an offer to present their research at a state conference. They feel intense anxiety about public speaking and, using affect as a guide, decline the invitation. The emotional response overrides an objective assessment of the professional benefit the opportunity would have provided.

subtopic.why: Heuristics underlie a vast range of everyday decisions, from choosing what to eat to how we assess risk. Understanding their positive and negative influences reveals why human decision-making is simultaneously efficient and prone to systematic error.

items.title: I can define prejudice and explain its relationship to stereotypes using the tri-component model of attitudes
items.what: Prejudice is an often negative preconception held against members of a particular group or social category. Within the tri-component model, prejudice corresponds to the affective component: it is the reflexive emotional feeling that arises from stereotypes, which are the cognitive component.
items.why: Locating prejudice within the tri-component model clarifies its relationship to both stereotypes and discrimination. A person can hold a stereotype without feeling prejudice, but stereotypes are the usual cognitive precursor to it.
items.example: The stereotype that homeless people are lazy (cognitive) may produce a feeling of contempt or avoidance when walking past someone sleeping rough (affective, prejudice). The stereotype provides the content; the prejudice is the emotional charge attached to it.

subtopic.name: Prejudice, Discrimination, and Stigma
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines prejudice, discrimination, and stigma, explains their relationships to one another, and positions them within the tri-component model of attitudes. It also covers direct and indirect discrimination, and the distinction between social stigma and self-stigma.
subtopic.why: These three phenomena cause measurable harm to individuals and communities. Precise understanding of how they differ and interrelate is necessary both for the VCE exam and for informed civic participation.

items.title: I can define discrimination and distinguish between direct and indirect forms
items.what: Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their membership in a social category. Direct discrimination involves treating an individual unfairly because of their group membership. Indirect discrimination occurs when a policy or rule applies to everyone but disproportionately disadvantages a particular group.
items.why: The distinction between direct and indirect discrimination is legally and socially significant. Indirect discrimination is harder to identify and challenge because it often appears neutral on the surface, yet its effects are not.
items.example: Direct: a hiring manager rejects a qualified applicant upon learning the applicant has a physical disability, assuming they will require too much time off. Indirect: a company policy requiring all staff to work Saturdays indirectly disadvantages employees whose religious observance prevents Saturday work.

items.title: I can position stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination within the tri-component model of attitudes
items.what: In the tri-component model applied to social group attitudes, stereotypes occupy the cognitive component (beliefs about the group), prejudice occupies the affective component (feelings toward the group), and discrimination occupies the behavioural component (actions toward group members).
items.why: This mapping clarifies the relationship between the three concepts. Each one corresponds to a distinct layer of an attitude, and they reinforce each other: cognitive stereotypes generate affective prejudice, which in turn produces behavioural discrimination.
items.example: Cognitive stereotype: 'Older workers are resistant to new technology.' Affective prejudice: feeling impatient or dismissive when an older colleague asks a technology-related question. Behavioural discrimination: excluding the older colleague from a project because the manager assumes they will struggle with the software.

items.title: I can define stigma and distinguish between social stigma and self-stigma
items.what: Stigma is the feeling of shame or disgrace experienced by an individual because of a characteristic that sets them apart from others. Social stigma refers to the widespread negative labelling of a group by society, leading to exclusion and discrimination. Self-stigma occurs when a person internalises these negative societal views about their own characteristic, leading to reduced self-efficacy and self-esteem.
items.why: Self-stigma is particularly harmful because it operates internally and can prevent individuals from seeking help, taking opportunities, or developing a realistic sense of their own capabilities. It is a mechanism through which social inequality is reproduced at the individual psychological level.
items.example: Social stigma: a person with a diagnosed mental health condition is assumed by colleagues to be unpredictable and incapable of leadership roles. Self-stigma: that same person begins to believe these assumptions are true and removes themselves from consideration for a leadership position they are objectively qualified for.

items.title: I can explain how the representative heuristic can contribute to prejudice and discrimination
items.what: When a person is categorised using the representative heuristic based on their perceived group membership, and that group is associated with negative stereotypes, the resulting categorisation can directly produce prejudiced feelings and discriminatory behaviour toward that individual.
items.why: This connection shows that prejudice is not only an emotional or moral failing but also a cognitive one, arising from normal mental shortcuts applied to social groups. It underscores why reducing prejudice requires addressing stereotypes and heuristic thinking, not just attitudes.
items.example: A security guard sees a young man wearing a hoodie and carrying a backpack in a shopping centre. Using the representative heuristic, the guard categorises him as belonging to a group associated with shoplifting and follows him. The man has done nothing suspicious and is purchasing a birthday gift.

items.title: I can define mental wellbeing and describe the characteristics of a person with optimal mental wellbeing
items.what: Mental wellbeing is an individual's current psychological state, encompassing their ability to think clearly, process information, and regulate emotions. A person with optimal mental wellbeing is able to make decisions, apply logic, maintain high self-esteem, stay optimistic, and experience low levels of stress and anxiety.
items.why: Establishing what optimal mental wellbeing looks like provides a baseline against which the negative effects of prejudice, discrimination, and stigma can be measured and assessed. It also clarifies what is at stake when these phenomena are left unaddressed.
items.example: A person with optimal mental wellbeing who encounters a setback at work is able to regulate their emotional response, assess options logically, seek support if needed, and maintain confidence in their ability to resolve the situation. A person whose wellbeing has been damaged by sustained discrimination may struggle with each of these responses.

subtopic.name: Mental Wellbeing and Reducing Harm
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the impacts of prejudice, discrimination, and stigma on the mental wellbeing of both individuals and groups. It also covers four evidence-based approaches to reducing these harms: education, inter-group contact, social media advocacy, and legislation.
subtopic.why: Prejudice and stigma are not abstract concepts: they produce measurable harm to psychological health. Understanding both the harm and the tools for reducing it is essential for applying psychology to real-world social issues.

items.title: I can identify and explain the negative effects of prejudice, discrimination, and stigma on personal mental wellbeing
items.what: Experiencing prejudice, discrimination, and stigma can damage personal mental wellbeing in several ways, including damaged self-image and self-confidence, heightened stress, increased rumination (dwelling on negative thoughts), and increased vulnerability to mental health disorders such as anxiety and depression.
items.why: These effects are cumulative: repeated exposure to discrimination compounds harm over time. Understanding them contextualises mental health disparities observed in marginalised communities and counters narratives that attribute those disparities solely to individual factors.
items.example: A student who is repeatedly mocked for their accent develops chronic anxiety about speaking in class. Over time, they begin to ruminate on these interactions outside school hours, experience declining self-confidence in academic settings, and eventually receive a diagnosis of social anxiety disorder.

items.title: I can identify and explain the negative effects of prejudice, discrimination, and stigma on group mental wellbeing
items.what: At the group level, prejudice, discrimination, and stigma can produce higher rates of mental health disorders across an entire community, feelings of social isolation from other groups, increased rates of substance abuse, fear of hate crimes when in public, and barriers to accessing mental health treatment due to stigma surrounding help-seeking.
items.why: Group-level effects show that the harm caused by discrimination is not simply the sum of individual harms. Community-wide psychological damage affects cultural cohesion, economic participation, and collective wellbeing in ways that persist across generations.
items.example: Research on the mental health of First Nations communities in Australia has documented elevated rates of psychological distress, substance use, and suicide compared to the broader population, with historical and ongoing discrimination identified as significant contributing factors.

items.title: I can describe how education can reduce prejudice, discrimination, and stigma
items.what: Education reduces prejudice by correcting misinformation and challenging the unfounded assumptions that underpin stereotypes. Exposure to accurate information about a group replaces the distorted cognitive content of stereotypes with more nuanced and evidence-based understanding.
items.why: Because stereotypes are learned, they can also be unlearned through new information. Education intervenes at the cognitive level and is therefore one of the most fundamental long-term strategies for prejudice reduction.
items.example: A school runs a series of workshops led by community members with lived experience of mental illness, sharing accurate information about the daily realities of managing a mental health condition. Students who attend report more empathetic and less fearful attitudes toward peers with mental health diagnoses.

items.title: I can explain how inter-group contact can reduce prejudice, discrimination, and stigma
items.what: Inter-group contact reduces prejudice through direct interaction between members of different social groups. Open conversation, respectful questioning, and genuine listening allow individuals to see beyond group stereotypes and recognise the individuality of people they might otherwise have categorised and dismissed.
items.why: Contact theory, with a substantial evidence base, shows that under certain conditions (equal status, shared goals, institutional support, cooperative activity) inter-group contact reliably reduces prejudice. Without those conditions, contact can sometimes reinforce prejudice.
items.example: A university organises paired mentoring between domestic and international students. Sustained one-on-one interaction over a semester reduces reported negative stereotypes among domestic students and increases international students' reported sense of belonging on campus.

items.title: I can explain how social media and legislation can each contribute to reducing prejudice and discrimination
items.what: Social media raises awareness of prejudice and discrimination at scale by amplifying personal accounts and calling out harmful behaviour publicly. Legislation reduces discrimination by creating formal legal consequences for discriminatory behaviour and providing recourse for those who are targeted.
items.why: These two approaches operate at different levels: social media shifts cultural norms through visibility and social accountability, while legislation enforces minimum standards of conduct regardless of cultural norms. Both are necessary, and neither is fully effective without the other.
items.example: Social media: a person shares a recorded incident of workplace discrimination on a public platform, prompting a company policy review and a public apology after widespread attention. Legislation: the Age Discrimination Act 2004 (Australia) provides a legal mechanism for employees over 50 to challenge unfair dismissal or non-selection based on age.
